items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
items.summary: Agent Retrieval in Vertex AI introduces managed ingestion and SearchDocuments to replace custom chunking and embedding pipelines. Developers can now import document and video files directly from Cloud Storage and query them with a single API call for cited page numbers and timestamped results. The feature supports hybrid retrieval, metadata filtering, reranking, and multimodal video audio search.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: How to handle user, connector, and agent auth in Gemini Enterprise with a custom UI
items.summary: When building a custom enterprise UI on top of Gemini Enterprise's :streamAssist API, developers must manually implement three core authentication layers. These include authenticating users or workloads via Google Identity or Workforce/Workload Identity Federation, managing third-party 3-legged OAuth (3LO) for Federated Connectors through the Keystore, and configuring on-demand per-tool OAuth for custom ADK agents using Vertex AI Agent Engine and GCP Auth Manager.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
items.summary: How to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP MCP servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect, FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 authentication.

items.title: Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs
items.summary: This post walks developers through training a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix and Gemma 4 on Cloud TPUs. By leveraging agentic Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and asynchronous vLLM rollouts, the approach significantly improves complex reasoning and tool compliance in interactive environments.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
items.summary: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
items.summary: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch

Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.summary: .NET Framework 4.8 has no end date: it is patched for as long as the Windows it runs on. It will also never get another feature. Moving to .NET 10 LTS is usually a series of small steps, not a rewrite, and the app keeps shipping while it happens. net10.0 enable .NET Framework 4.8.1 is the last version of .NET Framework, released in August 2022. Microsoft treats 4.8.1, 4.8 and 4.7.x as components of Windows, so they are supported and patched for as long as the Windows version they are installed on. There is no announced end-of-life date, and running a 4.8 app today is not running unsupported software. What 4.8 will not get is anything new. C# language versions, performance work, new ASP.NET Core and Entity Framework Core features, Linux and container support all happen in modern .NET: .NET 10 today. Library authors are following, and more NuGet packages ship new versions only for modern .NET each year. So the risk is not a deadline. Newer versions follow the support of Windows; older ones have their own end dates.

TypeScript 5.0 shipped standard decorators in March 2023, and three years later the ecosystem split is clear. The emitDecoratorMetadata compiler flag only works with legacy decorators enabled via experimentalDecorators. Standard decorators ignore the flag entirely because the TC39 proposal omitted type-directed metadata from the specification. Frameworks like NestJS, TypeORM, and InversifyJS rely on runtime type reflection to wire dependencies, and that reflection depends on emitDecoratorMetadata emitting design:type, design:paramtypes, and design:returntype keys that the reflect-metadata polyfill reads. Without it, the constructor argument @Inject(UserService) private users: UserService has no way to know that UserService is the type at runtime. The choice facing teams is to stay locked in legacy mode or migrate to manual metadata patterns that standard decorators support. items.summary: Order notifications that arrive twice are a common complaint in WhatsApp order flows. The template is fine, the integration works, but the customer gets the same "your order is confirmed" twice, or three times, and the support inbox fills with "why did I get this again?". The cause is almost never the messaging step. It is the webhook step. Store platforms such as Shopify send a webhook and wait for a fast 2xx response. If your endpoint is slow, times out, or the connection drops after the store sent the payload, the platform retries. Some retries come minutes later, some hours later. A manual replay from the admin panel adds another copy. The same event can reach you two or three times, and each delivery looks identical to the last one. If your handler turns every delivery into a message, every retry becomes another WhatsApp message. items.title: One typo in a timezone could stop every scheduled job in Rerun
items.summary: timezone: "Eastern" looks harmless. In Rerun it was saved without a word, and on the scheduler's next pass it could throw an error that kept every job lined up after it from even being checked. I came across it while reading the source. The report is issue #21 and the fix is rerun-build/rerun#22. Rerun lets you host your own team of digital coworkers, each handling jobs from your tools on a timetable. A coworker's repeating jobs are its routines. Each routine has a cron expression (0 9 * * * means 9:00 every day) and, optionally, a timezone. Valid timezone names come from the IANA list, things like Europe/Paris, plus a few aliases such as UTC. Every 30 seconds the engine runs a tick: it loops over all routines of all active coworkers and fires the ones that are due. To know if a routine is due, it asks croner, the cron library, for the next run. It's a bit like a booking form that happily accepts "Febtember 31". items.title: Next.js "Hydration failed because the initial UI does not match": 6 causes, the fix, and the one that leaks a key
items.summary: Your Next.js app shows this in the console, usually after you deploy or add a new component: Error: Hydration failed because the initial UI does not match what was rendered on the server. or "Text content does not match server-rendered HTML". The page may flash, break, or work after a refresh. Here is what it means, and the one "fix" that creates a security problem. Next.js renders your page to HTML on the server, then React "hydrates" it in the browser: it attaches events and expects the same markup. items.title: Why LibraryImport survives obfuscation
items.summary: Migrating from [DllImport] to [LibraryImport] is sold as a performance story — ahead-of-time-friendly marshalling, no IL stub generated at runtime, trim-safe. There is a quieter consequence that matters just as much if you obfuscate: the source generator changes where the native entry-point name lives, and in doing so it turns P/Invoke from one of the most rename-hostile surfaces in .NET into one of the safest. A native call has exactly one string that must survive: the export name the operating system loader looks up. With classic [DllImport], that string is often your method's own name. Write [DllImport("user32.dll")] static extern int MessageBoxW(...) with no EntryPoint, and the runtime uses the managed name MessageBoxW as the export to resolve. Rename the method and you have renamed the lookup key — the call throws EntryPointNotFoundException at runtime, with nothing wrong at build time. (That path, and the rule an obfuscator follows for it, is the subject of obfuscating P/Invoke without breaking interop.) items.title: Why Does Vite Run on localhost:5173? It's Not Random!
items.summary: React project run on localhost:3000. Then you start a Vite project, and suddenly it's localhost:5173. 🤔 Why such a random number? I finally looked it up, and it's not random at all. Think of your computer as an apartment building. In real life On your computer The building localhost (your own machine) A flat number The port The person living there Your running app So localhost:5173 simply means: "Go to my building and knock on flat 5173." Squint a little and read it like this: Number Letter Why 5 V Roman numeral for 5 1 I Looks like I 7 T Looks like T 3 E A flipped E 5173 = VITE ⚡ It's like a personalised number plate. At first you see digits, then you spot the name, and you can't unsee it. Here's the part I didn't know: earlier versions of Vite used port 3000 too. In Vite 3, the team changed the default to 5173 to move away from such a commonly used port. Imagine flat 3000 is the most popular flat in the building. Many tools want to move in, but for a given address, only one can live there at a time. So Vite packed its bags and moved to a flat with its own name on it. 📦 Why was 3000 picked in the first place? I couldn't find a confirmed reason. It's like a popular hangout spot.

It solved an industrial parts-tracking problem brilliantly. items.title: Stop Cursor Forgetting Your Database Schema (EF Core Guide)
items.summary: Ask Cursor for a query against a table it touched yesterday and it may still guess the column name, invent a navigation property, or write a migration for a column that already exists. It looks like forgetting. It's actually something simpler: the agent never had your schema in the first place, and every new chat starts empty. This guide shows how to put an accurate, compact version of your EF Core schema where the agent will read it, keep it from going stale, and make your project rules stick at the same time. Language models don't retain memory between sessions; Cursor's own docs say so plainly, and that's why rules exist. Within a session, the agent only knows what it has read. On an EF Core codebase, the schema is spread across places it rarely reads together: Entity classes give property names, which are not necessarily column names. Fluent configuration (IEntityTypeConfiguration , OnModelCreating) renames tables and columns, sets keys, owned types, value conversions and query filters. Conventions decide everything nobody configured explicitly, and they're invisible in the code. Migrations record how the schema got here, across dozens of files the agent has no reason to open.

items.title: Cursor for C# and .NET in 2026: Extensions, Debugging, Unity
items.summary: The first hour of C# in Cursor is more confusing than it should be. You open a solution, Cursor offers extensions you've never heard of, the one you use in VS Code isn't there, and the debugger behaves slightly differently. None of it is hard once you know why. This guide covers the licensing reason behind it, the three C# extensions that do work, a debugging setup that holds up on real solutions, Unity projects, and the rules that make Cursor write C# the way your team does. Cursor is built on the open-source VS Code codebase, but several of Microsoft's most popular extensions are not open source. The C# Dev Kit, the official C# extension's proprietary pieces and the vsdbg debugger are licensed for use only in Microsoft products: Visual Studio, VS Code and their hosted variants. Since Microsoft tightened enforcement in April 2025, opening a C# project in a fork showed a message that the extension may be used only with Microsoft Visual Studio Code. Cursor's response was to rebuild the affected extensions on open alternatives. In May 2025 it published its own C# extension (publisher: Anysphere), with one notable swap: debugging uses Samsung's open-source netcoredbg instead of vsdbg.

items.title: Obfuscating a JSON source-generated context
items.summary: A [JsonSerializable] context is the serializer you reach for when you are about to obfuscate. The reflection-based path reads your live property names at runtime, so renaming CustomerRef to a turns your JSON into {"a":…}; the source-generated path resolves everything at compile time and reaches your members through typed delegates, so the rename is invisible on the wire. That much is well known. What is less obvious is how the generated context stays intact — and where it does not. The generator writes the serialization contract down in two kinds of thing: tokens that the renamer follows, and literals that it leaves exactly where they are. A source-generated JsonSerializerContext is rename-safe precisely when those two halves stay in step, and it desyncs the moment a code path sidesteps the context. So the question worth answering concretely is: what does the generator actually emit, which parts move under renaming and which do not, and how do you prove the halves still line up after Nebula runs? items.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
items.summary: Hi HN! I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious. So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves. I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back! It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions. items.title: Your Upgrade Passed Every Test. Your API Docs Still Broke.
items.summary: After moving a project to .NET 11, everything was green. Build, tests, app startup. Then the Swagger UI page refused to render. The cause is one default. OpenApiOptions.OpenApiVersion now defaults to OpenAPI 3.2 instead of 3.1, so /openapi/v1.json starts with "openapi": "3.2.0". The server returns 200 and logs nothing. The swagger-ui bundled in Swashbuckle.AspNetCore.SwaggerUI 10.1.4 and earlier only understands 3.0 and 3.1, so it gives up. Your tests won't catch this, because the server isn't broken. The contract format changed, and the people who notice are your consumers: client generators, gateway imports, someone else's contract tests. The full article covers: three fixes: update the UI package, pin to 3.1, or serve a 3.2 and a 3.1 document side by side (plus the ShouldInclude line that side-by-side setup needs) why pinning down to 3.0 swaps one breaking change for another what breaks in custom document and schema transformers after the move to Microsoft.OpenApi 3.x a five-minute test that fails your pipeline the next time a framework upgrade changes the document version Read the full article on Medium

items.title: Letting a coding agent on Linux build, test and debug an iOS app
items.summary: I run Claude Code and Codex on a Linux machine. For web and backend work that's fine. For iOS it breaks down fast: there's no Xcode on Linux, no simulator, so the agent writes Swift it can never compile, and I end up being the compiler, copying errors back and forth. I built a small tool for that, called box. This post is about what I learned making a remote Mac useful to an agent, not to a human. (Disclosure: box is my product, it's paid, and the link is at the end.) A human can scroll through a 2,000-line xcodebuild log and find the one red line. An agent burns context doing that and often fixes the wrong thing. What worked better was making each build return something short and structured: $ box build box: 1 compile error(s): App/Module0.swift:2:19: cannot convert value of type 'String' to specified type 'Int' 1 | import Foundation > 2 | let broken: Int = "x" 3 | struct Module0 { box: bj_5WO8cgwGaPXkXTit failed, 60s billed Tests come back the same way, as a count plus files the agent can open: $ box test box: tests 3 passed, 0 failed box: saved ./.box/out/bj_f-P-JW-6hWjR-OnA/test-summary.json box: saved ./.box/out/bj_f-P-JW-6hWjR-OnA/test.xcresult.zip box: bj_f-P-JW-6hWjR-OnA su

items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. [...] These tools can download files via BitTorrent, and the authors and Nvidia both agree that whether they also upload data to others depends on the settings used. According to the authors, Nvidia didn't prevent seeding altogether. "When Nvidia ran the BitTorrent client, Nvidia uploaded pieces of pirated book files to third parties during the downloading process (i.e., before the download was complete). Nvidia also 'seeded' pirated books (i.e., made available and uploaded parts of a completely downloaded file). While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads. The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. items.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
items.summary: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not. items.title: Why I Built a 6 MB Native Swift Screenshot & Offline OCR App for macOS (Instead of Electron)
items.summary: Like a lot of developers who moved from Windows to macOS, I missed one tiny daily habit: capturing a region of my screen and pinning it floating above my IDE or PDF reader. Existing Mac tools each solved part of the puzzle, but never quite the combination I wanted: Built-in macOS (Cmd+Shift+4) is fast, but has no floating desktop pins and no one-click OCR from the selection bar. Snipaste is great for pinning, but its Mac build isn't native Swift/AppKit and offline OCR sits behind a paid upgrade. CleanShot X is an incredible all-in-one suite for video recording and cloud sharing, but overkill if you only want fast static screenshots, markup, pins, and local text extraction. So I built Stillpin—a lightweight (~6–7 MB) native Swift & AppKit menu bar utility for macOS 14+. Here are three engineering lessons from building a native macOS capture utility that surprised me along the way. You don't need a cloud API or a heavy bundled ML runtime to extract clean text from screenshots on macOS. items.title: James T. Russell, Physicist Who Pioneered CD and DVD Technology, Dies At 95
items.summary: James T. items.title: I gave Claude's voice a hologram face: a free, open-source macOS app
items.summary: Inspired by Joi, the hologram from Blade Runner 2049, I built Visage: a small macOS app that gives a hologram face to the voice of the AI you already talk to. Start Claude's voice mode (or ChatGPT's), and a face floats on your desktop and speaks with that voice: lips in sync, alive between sentences. It listens while you talk, thinks once you have finished, then answers. It is free and open source (MIT), and macOS only (macOS 15 or later, Apple silicon and Intel). No API key, no server, no account. Visage never talks to the AI app: it taps the sound that app plays with a per-process Core Audio tap, mutes it, and plays it back itself about 150 ms later. That delay is the trick. The voice analysis has already "heard" what comes next, so the lips can move before the sound, the way a real speaker's do, instead of trailing behind it. In a conversation, 150 ms more before the answer goes unnoticed. Voice analysis without a model: energy, pitch (YIN), formants (LPC), fricatives and lip closures, in plain signal processing with Accelerate. items.title: “Available Offline.” On Which Device? Testing Offline Maps on Apple Watch
items.summary: Your iPhone finishes downloading the trail map. You leave it in the car. Two kilometers up the trail, you reach a fork and check your Apple Watch. The route line is there. Underneath it, an empty grid. Which way do you turn? I’d start with the same action a hiker takes: download a route on the iPhone and wait until the app says “Available offline.” Then I’d leave the iPhone behind, take the Watch offline, and open the route on the Watch for the first time. That last detail matters. If I open the map while I’m still at my desk, I may only prove that the Watch can display an area it loaded a minute ago. On the Watch, I’d check three things: At the fork: Can I see the junction and both branches clearly enough to choose a trail? Farther along: If I pan to a section I’ve never viewed and zoom in, does the map still draw underneath the route? After reopening the app: Can I get back to the same offline map with the phone still out of reach? items.title: SwiftUI or UIKit in 2026: which to use for an iPhone app
items.summary: For a new iPhone app in 2026, I start in SwiftUI and reach for UIKit only where SwiftUI still falls short. Most of my work as a freelance iOS developer is SwiftUI. It isn't an either-or choice: the two mix in one app, so the question is which one leads. Widgets are built with SwiftUI views through WidgetKit, and so are Live Activities on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island (Apple). One codebase across Apple's platforms: the same views run on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Vision Pro, with platform tweaks. Less code for the same screen: layouts, state and animation are declared, not wired by hand, so screens are quicker to build and to change. Rich text editing and other text work beyond what SwiftUI's text views offer. Very custom scrolling and list layouts, where you need control over every cell and every offset. Large existing UIKit apps, where rewriting working screens buys nothing. Libraries that only ship UIKit views, such as some SDKs for maps, video or ads. items.title: NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features
items.summary: The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports: It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. Read more of this story

items.title: Plato's Key (8 minute read)
items.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that neural networks converge toward a shared representation of reality. Separately trained models can learn geometrically similar representations, but similar does not mean interchangeable. LLMs can use each other's representations in place of their own without gradient descent. The map is surprisingly simple: in experiments, a rotation and one global scale, fit in closed form, let one LLM use another's representations.

items.title: Measuring RSI (12 minute read)
items.summary: Neither compute allocation nor human intervention measures whether an AI training algorithm improved. Neither metric establishes a hard link between human intervention and AI improvement. Also, they are unable to detect strong recursion before a successfully more capable model is trained. Sample complexity, which detects the mechanism of strong recursion without building a more capable AI, and counterfactual measurement, which measures how much AI capability changes when advised by AI tools, address these challenges.

items.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot To Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, "Gravity." The research has been published in Science Advances. "Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," [said Dr. Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics]. "While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block." items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. items.title: Swarms do not yet raise the roof (46 minute read)
items.summary: Swarm-based LLM configurations, coordinated groups of agents, deliver faster but less efficient results compared to single agents at equal token budgets. Adding more agents to a swarm introduces a performance penalty that grows with size, leading to quality degradation. Given fresh context resets, single agents outperform swarms, suggesting that current swarm strategies primarily accelerate compute rather than significantly enhancing capabilities.

items.title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (3 minute read)
items.summary: The Anthropic proof that VP≠VNP means that there is no way to find the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size. This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn't clear how they would help with the permanent. There is a $1 million prize for a solution to this problem.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
items.summary: Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.
